newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Actor Smith's popularity knows no racial boundaries.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Actor Smith's popularity knows no racial boundaries.

text.p: Will Smith might as well be from another planet.

Not only has he accomplished what few Earthlings would even attempt by succeeding simultaneously in Hollywood's big three industries of music, television and film; the black star is also popular enough to command more than $10 million per film and get roles conceived for white actors despite Hollywood's continued resistance to African Americans.

The 28-year-old actor/singer/writer is expected to be the big draw for "Men In Black," the much-awaited alien summer blockbuster opening in the United States on July 1 and Smith's second big science fiction film in as many years. He starred last summer in "Independence Day," another alien-infested film that was the biggest moneymaker in 1996.
"Aliens probably watch these movies and think I know something. There's probably an alien hit (contract) on me right now," Smith told Reuters in his typically playful way.

The movie industry came under attack from the black community last year when only one out of 166 nominations for the Academy Awards was for an African American. But while roles for black actors remain scant, Smith's box office appeal is launching him into the stratosphere.

"I think Hollywood still has a long way to go. A lot of studios underestimate the drawing power of African American actors and actors," said Frank Jordan, president of the California State Conference of National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People (NAACP) branches.
UNIQUE PERSONALITY MAKES BOX OFFICE DRAW
"Smith is very fortunate and has a unique personality that makes him a box office draw. He's very educated and talented and he's managed to stay grounded," Jordan said.
Smith himself attributes his appeal with white audiences to the fact that his films such as "Independence Day" and the 1995 "Bad Boys" were not marketed as "black films."

"They marketed 'Bad Boys' like 'Top Gun' or like any of their other movies. They didn't market it like a black movie. They completely ignored the fact that there were two black stars in the movie," he said.

But he is also quick to remind people he is black, joking that his "negroid" features have not been captured in the doll representing "J," his character in "Men In Black," who gets recruited by "K," played by Tommy Lee Jones, into a secret organisation that battles a population of aliens on Earth.

Smith achieved fame in the music business in 1986 as a rapper named The Fresh Prince, then went on to star in the hit television series, The Fresh Prince of Bel Air, which just completed its sixth season. Its popularity led him into films such as the critically acclaimed "Six Degrees of Separation."

Smith, who grew up in Pennsylvania, admits he is surprised by the dizzying speed of his career. "It feels a little weird when I go back home. People I know forever act kind of scared," he said. "It wasn't like that with the music or the television show. It's actually kind of scary because I wonder if people are going to expect another big hit like 'Independence Day'."
'WILD WEST' MOVIE PLANNED

Smith, who just signed a record deal with Columbia Records, is now planning to star in a movie version of the 1960's television series "The Wild, Wild West," in which he will play James T. West, the role created by Robert Conrad.
Some Holywood professionals say Smith is able to cross over into "white man's roles" because he is a good actor.

"He's a heck of an entertainer and he gives 100 percent. He has no colour. I dont watch him as a black actor. It doesn't really matter what colour he is. I'm just watching Will Smith," one agent said.

Barry Sonnenfeld, who directed "Men in Black" and plans to direct "The Wild, Wild West," said Smith's race will be noted, but not dwelled upon, in the Western. "Will's black. I think we're going to have to deal with that to a little extent. I don't think that's what the movie's about but I don't think you can ignore the fact that its taking place four years after the Civil War and I've got a hero who is a black man."

While agents and producers seem confident of Smith's staying power at the box office, he is more philosophical. "Sometimes you're driving down the freeway in the rain and there's one car out of hundreds of thousands that breaks down. One of these days, I know that's going to be me," he said.
Then he added, laughing, "Sounds pretty deep, right? Well, actually it's quite shallow but it sounded deep!"
Smith has plenty to be laughing about these days.
